## Findings

- **Label polarity: UNRESOLVED from data alone — do not hardcode an assumption.** Multivariate feature-importance analysis (RandomForest, 300 trees, 5-fold CV) shows `Engine_RPM` drives ~45% of the separation between classes, far more than any other metric (`Fuel_Pressure` 17%, `Lub_Oil_Temperature` 13%, the rest under 10% each). Class 0 (n=5,774) averages **higher** `Engine_RPM` (885.7 vs 737.5) and **lower** `Fuel_Pressure` (6.23 vs 6.90) than class 1 (n=9,854); the other four metrics differ only marginally between classes. Neither direction reads as an unambiguous fault signature — there's no dramatic oil-pressure collapse or coolant-temperature spike in either class, and "engine runs faster" is not inherently a fault pattern (it could equally indicate class 1 = idling/low-load and class 0 = normal-operation, or the reverse under different domain conventions). **This cannot be resolved by statistics alone; it requires either the dataset's original source/documentation (not present in this repo) or an explicit product decision.** Do not encode `Engine_Condition == 1` as "faulty" (or vice versa) anywhere in code without this being settled — see plan §12, add as new open question pending user input or an external source citation.
- **Multivariate class separability (plan §12 Q2 — RESOLVED, not the worst case):** 5-fold cross-validated AUC is **0.688 (logistic regression, standardized features)** and **0.699 (RandomForest, raw features)** — both well above the 0.5 random baseline, so the classes ARE separable from the six raw metrics, just weakly-to-moderately (not the "statistically indistinguishable" scenario Q2 worried about). A model trained directly on these six raw features has a realistic ceiling around AUC ~0.70. This is the direct motivation for plan §7A's derived features (z-scores, cross-sensor ratios, composite stress index) — they're needed to push meaningfully past this ceiling, not merely nice-to-have.
- **Validator rules R2-R4 (plan §4.1): DROP all three — no correlation evidence.** Every pairwise correlation in the matrix above has |r| <= 0.072 (max: `Coolant_Temperature`/`Lub_Oil_Temperature` at 0.072). This is far below the |r| >= 0.15 evidentiary bar the plan set. **Implement validator.py with R1 (stopped-engine consistency) plus range checks only; do not implement R2 (oil pressure vs. speed), R3 (coolant pressure vs. coolant temp), or R4 (oil/coolant temp coupling)** — the plan's §4.1 hard gate explicitly anticipated this outcome and specified this exact fallback. Note R1 itself cannot be validated against `data/train.csv` either (no `status` column, §3) — it can only be exercised once the Phase 5 simulator emits `status`.
- **`Coolant_Temperature` confirmed outlier — exactly 2 anomalous rows out of 15,628.** Checked directly: only 2 rows exceed 100 (values 195.5 and 118.4); every other row is under 96, consistent with the other engine temperatures in the dataset. These 2 rows are very likely sensor faults or unit errors in the source data, not genuine physical readings, and they currently single-handedly set `engine-physics.yaml`'s proposed hard upper bound (195.978) via the widening formula in `characterize_train_csv.py`. **Recommendation for Phase 1:** either (a) exclude these 2 rows from the range-derivation computation (treat as known bad data, re-derive the bound from the remaining 15,626 rows, which would land much closer to the p99.9-based estimate of ~92), or (b) keep the wide bound but flag it explicitly in `engine-physics.yaml`'s comment as accommodating 2 known outlier rows rather than representing a physically plausible ceiling. Do not silently accept 196°C as a normal coolant temperature.
